classification.difficultyReason: Requires inventing matching-boundary constructions beyond regular polygons and a general side-count argument covering every integer, with no construction scaffold supplied.

content.prompt: It is possible to tessellate the plane using copies of a single triangle, and also using copies of a single quadrilateral. Determine for which values of $n$ there exists an $n$-gon which tessellates the plane, and for any such $n$ give an example of an $n$-gon that suffices.

answer.short:
All integers $n\geq3$.

Triangles, squares, a suitable pentagon and regular hexagons provide the first cases. Matching teeth on suitable tiles give examples for every larger number of sides.
answer.worked:
An equilateral triangle, a square and a regular hexagon tessellate the plane. The pentagon shown also tessellates: two copies, joined along their longest sloping edges, form a parallelogram, and parallelograms tessellate.

The four lower figures give examples with $7$, $8$, $9$ and $10$ sides. Their protrusions match the recesses of adjacent copies; the clipped corner in the $7$-sided example matches a neighbouring corner. Translating copies fills the plane without gaps or overlaps.

Extend an existing tooth pattern on both the top and bottom boundaries, keeping the two boundaries matching. Append the new diagonal and vertical segments immediately after an existing tooth, without an intervening horizontal segment. Each added tooth increases the side count by $2$, so adding one to each boundary increases it by $4$.

Every integer $n\geq7$ has the form $7+4k$, $8+4k$, $9+4k$ or $10+4k$, where $k\geq0$. Thus these four constructions, together with the examples for $3$, $4$, $5$ and $6$, cover all integers $n\geq3$.

spec.description: Editable examples for three through ten sides. The pentagon and four toothed polygons reconstruct the supplied solution figures; triangle, square and regular hexagon make the referenced earlier cases explicit.
spec.mathematics: The pentagon has five genuine vertices. The four lower polygons have exactly seven, eight, nine and ten sides, respectively. Matching opposite boundary profiles permit tessellation; extending paired tooth patterns adds four sides.
